evaluation.positioning_hook: A CIA trainee who can outfight the system starts seeing her own life as a manipulated simulation, then has to stop the man who built her before he turns her into a weapon.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clean commercial engine: elite espionage training, a conspiracy reveal, and a final-act rooftop showdown in Washington, D.C. The emotional hook is legible and broad, though the dense tech vocabulary and layered reality concept narrow it slightly from four-quadrant simplicity.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and hard: ARC turns intelligence training into a reality-overwriting system, and Ridley begins to suspect her own life has been engineered. The opening Istanbul rescue, the Georgetown lecture, and the Farm reveal all stack the hook with strong clarity.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ridley is a strong lead because her competence is inseparable from her distrust of authority, and Ian gives the story a credible emotional counterweight. Dawson/West is a vivid antagonist, and the ensemble trainees each have a functional lane, though only Ridley is truly durable.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The ARC system, the card-based intelligence interface, and the idea of training the system while it trains you give the script a fresh sci-fi-thriller identity. The repeated cycle structure and the final memory recontextualization are bold choices that push beyond standard espionage plotting.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with real propulsion from the Istanbul op to the Farm reveal to the live D.C. mission. Each major sequence escalates the stakes or reframes the previous one, and the rooftop climax pays off the internal and external conflicts at once.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels immediately usable and distinct: a trauma-informed CIA recruit discovers her reality is being overwritten by a predictive warfare program. It’s familiar in the broad lane of paranoid sci-fi, but the specific intelligence-training architecture and coercive-control framing make it feel ownable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Farm, ARC backlot, neural patches, collection cards, and live-op integration create a world with rules and hierarchy, not just a backdrop. The intelligence ecosystem feels story-generating, especially with the tension between training, surveillance, and field deployment.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends sleek techno-thriller mechanics with emotional paranoia and a grounded espionage sensibility. The script knows when to be procedural, when to be intimate, and when to go full action set-piece, which gives it a distinct register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The cycle reveal, the memory architecture, and the possibility that Ridley’s entire life has been constructed give the script substantial hidden depth. The ending’s reset suggests a larger system and a deeper mythology without losing the immediate thriller payoff.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ridley/Ian is the engine, and the trainee ensemble gives the story recurring friction through rivalry and alliance. The relationships are functional and sometimes sharp, though the script still lives primarily on the central duo rather than a truly modular ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Ridley Cooper
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, elite intelligence trainee; psychologically resilient, trauma-affected, highly observant.
lead_characters.hook: A Georgetown psych prodigy turned CIA recruit, Ridley is the rare protagonist whose instinct is both her gift and her threat. She’s smart enough to see the seams in ARC, wounded enough to recognize coercion in real time, and stubborn enough to keep pushing even when the system rewrites her life around compliance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Natalie Portman in Black Swan or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve — a role that demands precision, vulnerability, and escalating psychological fracture. It gives an actor the chance to play intelligence as action, then turn that intelligence into the engine of a full-blown identity crisis.

lead_characters.name: Ian Walsh
lead_characters.demographics: Man, mid-20s to early 30s, CIA operative/trainee, physically capable, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: Ian is the program’s ideal product: disciplined, competitive, and deeply invested in the idea that the system can make him better. He starts as Ridley’s ally and mirror, but the script uses him as the emotional proof of what ARC can do when obedience replaces judgment.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Adam Driver in The Report or Miles Teller in Whiplash — a role built on controlled intensity, physical competence, and the slow reveal of what the character is willing to sacrifice to win. It gives an actor a clean arc from polished operator to compromised believer.

lead_characters.name: Cameron West
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s, professor/architect figure, authoritative, charismatic, psychologically predatory.
lead_characters.hook: West is the script’s human face of control: elegant, patient, and terrifying because he speaks in the language of care while engineering domination. He functions as both the abusive ex and the hidden architect of ARC, which makes him feel intimate and institutional at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Matthew Goode in The Offer a chance to weaponize calm. It’s a prestige villain part with real range: seductive, clinical, and finally monstrous.

lead_characters.name: Alvarez
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, data/analytics trainee, sharp, guarded, observant.
lead_characters.hook: Alvarez is the quiet intelligence in the room, the one who understands that certainty is often the least trustworthy thing in the system. She’s not written as comic relief or exposition delivery; she’s the ensemble’s clearest counterweight to ARC’s false confidence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Auli'i Cravalho in The Power or Stephanie Hsu in Everything Everywhere All at Once a chance to play intelligence with emotional restraint. It offers a smart, watchful performance that can steal scenes without needing the biggest speeches.

lead_characters.name: Egan
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, human intelligence trainee, legacy background, aggressive, status-driven.
lead_characters.hook: Egan is the recruit most seduced by ARC’s promise of certainty and dominance. He’s a useful antagonist inside the team because he believes the system is a meritocracy, which makes him both dangerous and tragically easy to manipulate.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Glen Powell in Devotion or Sebastian Stan in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier a chance to play swagger with a crack underneath. It’s a strong supporting turn for an actor who can sell charm, entitlement, and volatility in the same beat.

lead_characters.name: Dawson
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 40s, intelligence/defense technologist, polished, opaque, institutionally powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Dawson is the face ARC chooses to wear: calm, persuasive, and always a step ahead of the room. The script keeps him slippery on purpose, and that ambiguity is part of the pleasure because he can read as ally, handler, or predator depending on the scene.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Ben Mendelsohn in Bloodline or Paul Dano in Prisoners a chance to make menace feel civilized. It’s a prestige-supporting part with real scene-eating potential.

lead_characters.name: Sykes
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s-60s, operations director, senior intelligence authority, hard-edged.
lead_characters.hook: Sykes is the institutional pragmatist who treats people as assets and outcomes as the only moral language that matters. He’s not the mastermind; he’s the executive function that makes the machine feel real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave JK Simmons in Whiplash or Bryan Cranston in Argo a chance to command a room with authority and threat. It’s a sharp supporting part for an actor who can make bureaucracy feel dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Harrison
lead_characters.demographics: Man, older, lead trainer, veteran ops figure, disciplined and severe.
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the old-school trainer who believes pain, repetition, and obedience are the path to competence. He’s the human bridge between the Farm’s physical discipline and ARC’s more elegant control architecture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Nick Offerman in Devotion a chance to embody institutional pressure with precision. It’s a strong authority role with memorable command presence.

casting_characteristics: 20s lead with high physical and emotional range
ensemble of intelligence trainees with distinct skill profiles

notable_requirements: Washington, D.C. embassy and government exteriors
multiple simulated international environments created through AR/production design

technical.vfx_details: AR overlays, HUD interfaces, overwrite environments, digital recontextualization of spaces, and cycle-reset visual transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: gunfire, explosions, rooftop falls, vehicle hijack, practical combat choreography, simulated environment transitions

rights_flags.detail: Senator Kerrigan is a fictional character, but the script also references Senator Kennedy in the epilogue in a way that may invite real-person association.
Apple Watch is named in dialogue.
Uber is referenced in the trainee arrival sequence.
World Bank is named in dialogue.
CIA, DOD, Georgetown University, Veterans Affairs, and Camp Peary are all depicted as real organizations/locations.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or theatrical genre thriller
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: event thriller with franchise-adjacent packaging potential but designed to stand alone.

budget.note: Contemporary setting keeps it grounded, but the Istanbul opener, D.C. rooftop finale, multiple simulated international environments, and moderate VFX/HUD work will push above a simple contained-thriller spend.

casting.note: Ridley needs a lead who can carry action, psychological fracture, and procedural intelligence at once, while Ian and West each need strong, specific actors to make the central triangle land.

development.note: The cycle reveal and final reset are commercially strong, but the script asks the audience to track layered reality, memory manipulation, and institutional conspiracy without losing emotional clarity.

comp_set.title: The Bourne Identity
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the identity-paranoia engine and the sense of a protagonist discovering the system has been shaping them from the inside.

comp_set.title: Minority Report
comp_set.why_it_comps: The predictive-policing and pre-crime logic rhyme with ARC’s attempt to optimize human behavior before action happens.

comp_set.title: Source Code
comp_set.why_it_comps: The repeated-cycle structure and the emotional race against a system that keeps resetting reality are a close tonal and structural neighbor.

comp_set.title: Edge of Tomorrow
comp_set.why_it_comps: The training-to-combat escalation and iterative learning loop give it the same propulsive, game-like momentum.

comp_set.title: The Adjustment Bureau
comp_set.why_it_comps: The romance-plus-conspiracy lane and the idea of a hidden system shaping personal destiny are directly adjacent.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, high-concept espionage thrillers with a strong female lead and a romance/conspiracy spine.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing but broadly adult, with strong appeal to genre-literate streaming and theatrical thriller audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary espionage setting, moderate VFX for AR overlays and overwrites, plus a handful of international and action-heavy sequences.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams buying elevated genre
director-driven packages looking for a smart female-led franchise starter
lane_fit.detail: This sits in the lane where concept clarity, star-driven casting, and a clean trailer hook matter as much as the twist. The script has enough action and enough brain to attract buyers who want genre with a premium sheen.

ip_potential.detail: The ARC program and the cycle architecture create a sequelable universe, but the clearest spinoff vector is a prequel centered on West/Dawson building ARC inside the intelligence community.

strengths.dimension_or_area: ARC is a clean, ownable engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The card-based AR intelligence system gives the movie a trailer-friendly visual language and a marketable hook beyond standard spycraft. That makes it easier to sell to buyers who want a fresh mechanism, not just another conspiracy plot.
strengths.evidence: The backlot overwrite, the collection cards, and the HUD-driven training sequences all turn intelligence into a playable system.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ridley is a real star role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead combines action competence, psychological depth, and moral resistance, which is exactly the kind of part that can elevate a mid-budget package. That is the role type actors and reps chase when they want a franchise-capable female lead with awards-adjacent texture.
strengths.evidence: She beats the dojo test by ignoring the system, breaks into the server room, and ultimately refuses ARC’s version of reality.

strengths.what_it_means: The Ridley/Ian relationship gives the movie a human anchor inside the high-concept machinery, which broadens the audience beyond pure sci-fi buyers. It also gives casting a built-in chemistry test that can drive package momentum.
strengths.evidence: Their Columbia history, the rooftop recognition beat, and the final “Hey, Coop” moment all pay off the romance/conspiracy thread.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final-act reveal recontextualizes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The cycle structure and memory reset give the script a strong conversation piece and a rewatch factor, which helps both audience buzz and premium-platform positioning. It’s the kind of twist that can turn a good thriller into a word-of-mouth title.
strengths.evidence: The server-room discovery, the cycle logs, and the final CYCLE 3 INITIATED button-push all reframe the earlier story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels operational, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: The Farm, ARC, the trainees, and the live-op integration create a believable institutional ecosystem that supports both tension and scale. Buyers respond to worlds that generate scenes naturally, and this one does.
strengths.evidence: The training modules, leaderboards, live mission briefings, and after-action debrief all feel like a functioning machine.

whats_special.headline: This is a premium, high-concept espionage thriller with a genuinely sellable engine: a female-led CIA package, a fresh AR surveillance conceit, and a romance/conspiracy spine that gives the action emotional lift. It’s the kind of mid-budget genre play that can attract a strong lead, a prestige villain, and a streamer or theatrical buyer looking for smart spectacle with a clean hook.

items.area: The final-cycle reveal is a big swing.
items.detail: The script’s last-act recontextualization is ambitious and memorable, but it asks the audience to absorb a second reality architecture on top of an already layered conspiracy. That makes the ending a strong conversation piece and a real buyer question: the payoff is there, but the clarity burden is high.

ARC, cards, overwrites, HUMINT/SIGINT/GEOINT, and the repeated HUD logic create a rich system, but the script leans hard on terminology to explain itself. That’s a strength for genre buyers and a friction point for broader audiences who need the emotional stakes to stay ahead of the mechanics.

items.area: Ridley and Ian carry most of the engine.
items.detail: The trainee ensemble is functional, but the movie’s real momentum lives in the Ridley/Ian/Dawson triangle. That concentrates the casting and chemistry burden on three roles, which is manageable creatively but important for packaging conversations.

items.area: The action footprint is not tiny.
items.detail: Istanbul, the Farm, the D.C. embassy run, rooftop combat, vehicle hijacking, and multiple simulated international environments mean this is not a contained one-set thriller. It’s still mid-budgetable, but only if the buyer is comfortable with a real action-thriller spend and moderate VFX support.

items.area: The clearance lane is mostly clean, but not invisible.
items.detail: The script is original IP, but it does name Apple Watch, Uber, World Bank, Georgetown, CIA, DOD, Veterans Affairs, and Camp Peary, which means a legal pass is still needed on brand and real-organization usage. None of that is fatal, but it is real business affairs work before greenlight.

issues.headline: The main development conversation is not whether the script has a hook — it clearly does — but whether the audience can track the layered reality without losing the emotional thread. The other practical conversation is packaging: this wants a strong lead, a strong villain, and enough budget to make the AR world feel premium rather than merely explained.
